Single-Item Questions
A single patient-centered vignette is associated with one question followed by four or more response options.
The response options are lettered (A, B, C, D, E). A portion of the questions require interpretation of graphic
or pictorial materials. You are required to select the best answer to the question. Other options may be
partially correct, but there is only ONE BEST answer. This is the traditional, most frequently used multiple-
choice question format on the examination.
Strategies for Answering Single One-Best-Answer Test Questions
The following are strategies for answering one-best-answer items:
• Read each patient vignette and question carefully. It is important to understand what is being asked.
• Try to generate an answer and then look for it in the response option list.
• Alternatively, read each response option carefully, eliminating those that are clearly incorrect.
• Of the remaining options, select the one that is most correct.

• Alternatively, read each response option carefully, eliminating those that are clearly incorrect.
• Of the remaining options, select the one that is most correct.
• If unsure about an answer, it is better to guess since unanswered questions are automatically counted
as wrong answers.
Example Item
A 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus has had progressive renal failure during the past 2 years.
She has not yet started dialysis. Examination shows no abnormalities. Her hemoglobin concentration is 9 g/dL,
hematocrit is 28%, and mean corpuscular volume is 94 μm3. A blood smear shows normochromic, normocytic
cells. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
(A) Acute blood loss
(B) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
(C) Erythrocyte enzyme deficiency
(D) Erythropoietin deficiency
(E) Immunohemolysis
(F) Microangiopathic hemolysis
(G) Polycythemia vera
(H) Sickle cell disease
(I) Sideroblastic anemia
(J) β-Thalassemia trait
(Answer: D)

(D) Erythropoietin deficiency
(E) Immunohemolysis
(F) Microangiopathic hemolysis
(G) Polycythemia vera
(H) Sickle cell disease
(I) Sideroblastic anemia
(J) β-Thalassemia trait
(Answer: D)
NOTE: Some item types that appear on the Step 1 examination are NOT depicted in the sample items provided
in this booklet, eg, items with multimedia features, such as audio. Also, when additional item formats are
added to the exam, notice will be provided at the USMLE website: http://www.usmle.org. You must monitor
the website to stay informed about the types of items that occur in the exam, and you must practice with the
downloadable sample test items available on the USMLE website to be fully prepared for the examination.
USMLE STEP 1 TEST QUESTION FORMATS

4
The following pages include 119 sample test questions. Most of these questions are the same as those you can
install on your computer from the USMLE website. Please note that reviewing the sample questions as they
appear on pages 8–47 is not a substitute for practicing with the test software. You should download and run
the Step 1 tutorial and practice test items that are provided on the USMLE website well before your test date.
The sample materials available on the USMLE website include an additional item with associated audio
findings that does not appear in this booklet. You should become familiar with this item format that will be
used in the actual examination.
Although the sample questions exemplify content on the Step 1 examination overall, they may not reflect the
content coverage on individual examinations. In the actual examination, questions will be presented in
random order; they will not be grouped according to specific content. The questions will be presented one at a

random order; they will not be grouped according to specific content. The questions will be presented one at a
time in a format designed for easy on-screen reading, including use of the USMLE Laboratory Values table
(included here on pages 5–7) and some pictorials. Photographs, charts, and x-rays in this booklet are not of
the same quality as the pictorials used in the actual examination. In addition, you will be able to adjust the
brightness and contrast of pictorials on the computer screen.
To take the following sample test questions as they would be timed in the actual examination, you should
allow a maximum of 1 hour for each 40-item block, and a maximum of 58 minutes, 30 seconds, for the 39-item
block, for a total of 2 hours, 58 minutes, 30 seconds. Please note that the third block has 39 items instead of
40 because the multimedia item has been removed, and the recommended time to complete the block has

40 because the multimedia item has been removed, and the recommended time to complete the block has
been adjusted accordingly. Please be aware that most examinees perceive the time pressure to be greater
during an actual examination. All examinees are strongly encouraged to practice with the downloadable
version to become familiar with all item formats and exam timing. An answer form for recording answers is
provided on page 48. An answer key is provided on page 49. In the actual examination, answers will be
selected on the screen; no answer form will be provided.

USMLE STEP 1 SAMPLE TEST QUESTIONS
BLOCK 1, ITEMS 1-40
1. A 67-year-old woman with congenital bicuspid aortic valve is admitted to the hospital because of a 2-day history of
fever and chills. Current medication is lisinopril. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are
20/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a grade 3/6 systolic murmur that is best
heard over the second right intercostal space. Blood culture grows viridans streptococci susceptible to penicillin. In
addition to penicillin, an antibiotic synergistic to penicillin is administered that may help shorten the duration of this
patient's drug treatment. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of action of this additional antibiotic
on bacteria?
(A) Binding to DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
(B) Binding to the 30S ribosomal protein
(C) Competition with p-aminobenzoic acid
(D) Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase
(E) Inhibition of DNA gyrase

(A) Binding to DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
(B) Binding to the 30S ribosomal protein
(C) Competition with p-aminobenzoic acid
(D) Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase
(E) Inhibition of DNA gyrase
2. A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-month history of intermittent yellowing of the eyes and
skin. Physical examination shows no abnormalities except for jaundice. Her serum total bilirubin concentration is
3 mg/dL, with a direct component of 1 mg/dL. Serum studies show a haptoglobin concentration and AST and ALT
activities that are within the reference ranges. There is no evidence of injury or exposure to toxins. Which of the
following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
(A) Decreased activity of UDP glucuronosyltransferase
(B) Gallstones
(C) Increased hemolysis
(D) Increased serum alkaline phosphatase activity
(E) Ineffective erythropoiesis

(A) Decreased activity of UDP glucuronosyltransferase
(B) Gallstones
(C) Increased hemolysis
(D) Increased serum alkaline phosphatase activity
(E) Ineffective erythropoiesis
3. During an experiment, drug X is added to a muscle bath containing a strip of guinea pig intestinal smooth muscle.
Agonists are added to the bath, and the resultant effects on muscle tension are shown in the table.
Agonist Muscle Tension Before Drug X (g) Muscle Tension After Drug X (g)
Vehicle 6.0 6.1
Acetylcholine 11.3 18.5
Norepinephrine 4.1 4.2
Which of the following types of drugs is most likely to produce effects most similar to those of drug X?
(A) α1-Adrenergic antagonist
(B) β-Adrenergic antagonist
(C) Cholinesterase inhibitor
(D) Monoamine oxidase inhibitor
(E) Muscarinic antagonist

9
4. A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 0, aborta 1, at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the office for a prenatal visit. She
has had one previous pregnancy resulting in a spontaneous abortion at 12 weeks' gestation. Today, her vital signs are
within normal limits. Physical examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 28-week gestation. Fetal
ultrasonography shows a male fetus with no abnormalities. Her blood group is O, Rh-negative. The father's blood
group is B, Rh-positive. The physician recommends administration of Rh o(D) immune globulin to the patient. This
treatment is most likely to prevent which of the following in this mother?
(A) Development of natural killer cells
(B) Development of polycythemia
(C) Formation of antibodies to RhD
(D) Generation of IgM antibodies from fixing complement in the fetus
(E) Immunosuppression caused by RhD on erythrocytes from the fetus

(C) Formation of antibodies to RhD
(D) Generation of IgM antibodies from fixing complement in the fetus
(E) Immunosuppression caused by RhD on erythrocytes from the fetus
5. A 55-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of shortness of breath and confusion for
4 hours. He has hypertension and chronic kidney disease requiring hemodialysis. An ECG shows low voltage with
electrical alternans. Physical examination is most likely to show which of the following findings?
Blood Pressure Jugular Venous Pulsus
(mm Hg) Pulse (/min) Pressure Paradoxus
(A) 85/60 120 increased increased
(B) 85/60 120 increased normal
(C) 85/60 120 normal normal
(D) 120/80 80 increased increased
(E) 120/80 80 normal increased
(F) 120/80 80 normal normal
6. A 52-year-old woman begins pharmacotherapy after being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Four weeks
later, her hepatic glucose output is decreased, and target tissue glucose uptake and utilization are increased. Which

later, her hepatic glucose output is decreased, and target tissue glucose uptake and utilization are increased. Which
of the following drugs was most likely prescribed for this patient?
(A) Acarbose
(B) Glyburide
(C) Metformin
(D) Nateglinide
(E) Repaglinide

10
7. An asymptomatic 44-year-old man is found to have HIV infection during routine screening prior to donating blood.
A complete blood count done at the time of the screening shows:
Hemoglobin 10 g/dL
Hematocrit 30%
Leukocyte count 4600/mm3
Platelet count 15,000/mm3
Prothrombin time 12 sec (INR=1.1)
Partial thromboplastin time 23 sec
Which of the following physical findings is most likely in this patient?
(A) Deep venous thrombosis
(B) Hemarthrosis
(C) Petechiae
(D) Subungual hemorrhage
(E) Visceral hematoma
8. A 23-year-old woman with bone marrow failure is treated with a large dose of rabbit antithymocyte globulin. Ten
days later, she develops fever, lymphadenopathy, arthralgias, and erythema on her hands and feet. Which of the
following is the most likely cause of these symptoms?
(A) Cytokine secretion by natural killer cells
(B) Eosinophil degranulation
(C) Immune complex deposition in tissues
(D) Polyclonal T-lymphocyte activation
(E) Widespread apoptosis of B lymphocytes

(A) Cytokine secretion by natural killer cells
(B) Eosinophil degranulation
(C) Immune complex deposition in tissues
(D) Polyclonal T-lymphocyte activation
(E) Widespread apoptosis of B lymphocytes
9. After being severely beaten and sustaining a gunshot wound to the abdomen, a 42-year-old woman undergoes
resection of a perforated small bowel. During the operation, plastic reconstruction of facial fractures, and open
reduction and internal fixation of the left femur are also done. Thirty-six hours postoperatively, she is awake but not
completely alert. She is receiving intravenous morphine via a patient-controlled pump. She says that she needs the
morphine to treat her pain, but she is worried that she is becoming addicted. She has no history of substance use
disorder. She drinks one to two glasses of wine weekly. Which of the following initial actions by the physician is
most appropriate?
(A) Reassure the patient that her chance of becoming addicted to narcotics is minuscule

most appropriate?
(A) Reassure the patient that her chance of becoming addicted to narcotics is minuscule
(B) Maintain the morphine, but periodically administer intravenous naloxone
(C) Switch the patient to oral acetaminophen as soon as she can take medication orally
(D) Switch the patient to intramuscular lorazepam
(E) Switch the patient to intravenous phenobarbital

11
10. A 22-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 4-day history of an itchy, red rash on her right arm. She has
no history of major medical illness and takes no medications. She says she has recently used a new hair dye. She is
165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 61 kg (135 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m 2. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is
70/min. respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. Examination of the right forearm shows the
findings in the photograph. Which of the following ligand → receptor pairs most likely played a primary role in the
proliferation of the T lymphocytes present at the site of the rash in this patient?
(A) CD2 on T lymphocytes → intercellular adhesion molecule (ICAM)-3 on epidermal Langerhans cells
(B) CD28 on T lymphocytes → CD80 on epidermal Langerhans cells
(C) CD40L on T lymphocytes → CD40 on epidermal Langerhans cells
(D) CD45 on T lymphocytes → CD28 on epidermal Langerhans cells

(B) CD28 on T lymphocytes → CD80 on epidermal Langerhans cells
(C) CD40L on T lymphocytes → CD40 on epidermal Langerhans cells
(D) CD45 on T lymphocytes → CD28 on epidermal Langerhans cells
(E) Lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 on T lymphocytes → ICAM1 on epidermal Langerhans cells
11. Six healthy subjects participate in a study of muscle metabolism during which hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia
is induced. Muscle biopsy specimens obtained from the subjects during the resting state show significantly increased
concentrations of malonyl-CoA. The increased malonyl-CoA concentration most likely directly inhibits which of the
following processes in these subjects?
(A) Fatty acid oxidation
(B) Fatty acid synthesis
(C) Gluconeogenesis
(D) Glycogenolysis
(E) Glycolysis
(F) Oxidative phosphorylation
12. Over 1 year, a study is conducted to assess the antileukemic activity of a new tyrosine kinase inhibitor in patients

(D) Glycogenolysis
(E) Glycolysis
(F) Oxidative phosphorylation
12. Over 1 year, a study is conducted to assess the antileukemic activity of a new tyrosine kinase inhibitor in patients
with chronic myeloid leukemia in blast crisis. All patients enrolled in the study are informed that they would be
treated with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor. They are assigned to successive dose cohorts of 300 to 1000 mg/day of the
drug. Six to eight patients are assigned to each dose. Treatment efficacy is determined based on the results of
complete blood counts and bone marrow assessments conducted regularly throughout the study. This study is best
described as which of the following?
(A) Case-control study
(B) Crossover study
(C) Open-labeled clinical trial
(D) Randomized clinical trial
(E) Single-blind, randomized, controlled trial

12
13. A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 4-day history of increasingly severe left leg
pain and swelling of his left calf. He also has a 1-month history of increasingly severe upper midthoracic back pain.
During this time, he has had a 9- kg (20-lb) weight loss despite no change in appetite. He has no history of major
medical illness. His only medication is ibuprofen. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11
 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is
25 kg/m2. His vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, lower extremity pulses are palpable bilaterally.
The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the thoracic spine shows no
abnormalities. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a 3-cm mass in the body of the pancreas; there are liver metastases
and encasement of the superior mesenteric artery. Ultrasonography of the left lower extremity shows a

and encasement of the superior mesenteric artery. Ultrasonography of the left lower extremity shows a
femoropopliteal venous clot. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
(A) Carcinoid syndrome
(B) Hypercoagulability from advanced malignancy
(C) Multiple endocrine neoplasia
(D) Splenic artery aneurysm and embolic disease of the left lower extremity
(E) Superior mesenteric artery syndrome
14. A 40-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of increased facial hair growth. Her last
menstrual period was 4 months ago. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 70 kg (154 lb); BMI is 26 kg/m 2. Her
pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 130/82 mm Hg. Physical examination shows temporal balding and coarse dark
hair on the upper lip and chin. Pelvic examination shows clitoral enlargement. Her serum testosterone concentration
is increased. Serum concentrations of androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone, and urinary 17-ketosteroids are

is increased. Serum concentrations of androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone, and urinary 17-ketosteroids are
within the reference ranges. Ultrasonography of the pelvis shows a 12-cm ovarian mass. Which of the following best
describes this mass?
(A) Granulosa tumor
(B) Ovarian carcinoid
(C) Sertoli-Leydig tumor
(D) Teratoma
(E) Thecoma
15. A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain and swelling of his right arm where he scraped it on a
tree branch 2 days ago. His temperature is 38.3°C (101°F). Examination of the right forearm shows edema around a
fluctuant erythematous lesion at the site of trauma. The area is extremely tender to palpation. Which of the following
is most likely the primary mechanism of the development of edema in this patient?
(A) Degranulation of eosinophils
(B) Disruption of vascular basement membranes
(C) Increased hydrostatic pressure
(D) Release of thromboxane
(E) Separation of endothelial junctions

(A) Degranulation of eosinophils
(B) Disruption of vascular basement membranes
(C) Increased hydrostatic pressure
(D) Release of thromboxane
(E) Separation of endothelial junctions
16. A 12-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-month history of headaches and a 6-day history of
nausea and vomiting. Funduscopic examination shows bilateral papilledema. He walks with a broad-based gait. An
MRI of the brain shows a tumor in the pineal region compressing the brain stem and leading to hydrocephalus. This
patient most likely has impairment of which of the following oculomotor functions?
(A) Abduction
(B) Horizontal pursuit
(C) Optokinetic nystagmus
(D) Upward gaze
(E) Vestibulo-ocular reflex

13
17. A 52-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of nausea, vomiting, and right-
sided abdominal pain that radiates to his back. He has not had fever or increased urinary frequency. He has a history
of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and atrial fibrillation. Current medications are

Single-Item Questions
A single patient-centered vignette is associated with one question followed by four or more response options.
The response options are lettered (A, B, C, D, E). A portion of the questions require interpretation of graphic
or pictorial materials. You are required to select the best answer to the question. Other options may be
partially correct, but there is only ONE BEST answer. This is the traditional, most frequently used multiple-
choice question format on the examination.
Strategies for Answering Single One-Best-Answer Test Questions
The following are strategies for answering one-best-answer items:
• Read each patient vignette and question carefully. It is important to understand what is being asked.
• Try to generate an answer and then look for it in the response option list.
• Alternatively, read each response option carefully, eliminating those that are clearly incorrect.
• Of the remaining options, select the one that is most correct.

• Alternatively, read each response option carefully, eliminating those that are clearly incorrect.
• Of the remaining options, select the one that is most correct.
• If unsure about an answer, it is better to guess since unanswered questions are automatically counted
as wrong answers.

lumbar puncture is performed. Results of cerebrospinal fluid analysis show cysts and trophozoites. The most likely
portal of pathogen entry into this patient's central nervous system is which of the following?

facial expression at a party. His pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg. He is sitting upright and

two groups: 2500 patients receive the new drug and 2500 patients receive placebo. If the alpha is set at 0.01 instead

6 months. The patient is unconcerned about the lack of menses. Menarche occurred at the age of 12 years, and

school gymnastics team. She appears emaciated. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 40 kg (88 lb); BMI is

103. A male stillborn is delivered at 32 weeks' gestation to a 30-year-old woman. The pregnancy was complicated by
oligohydramnios. Examination of the stillborn shows the absence of a urethral opening. Which of the following

(A) Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
(B) Intralobar sequestration
(C) Pulmonary hypoplasia
(D) Situs inversus

irritability since delivery, and a 2-hour history of vomiting. Physical examination shows jaundice and hepatomegaly.
A reducing substance test result of the urine is positive, and a glucose oxidase test result is negative. The

camping trip in New Mexico. He appears ill and lethargic and can barely answer questions. His temperature is
39.2°C (102.5°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Physical

39.2°C (102.5°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Physical
examination shows generalized scattered black maculae. Examination of the right upper extremity shows an
erythematous, solid, tender mass on the underside of the upper extremity just above the elbow; the mass is draining
blood and necrotic material. The most effective antibiotic for this patient’s disorder will interfere with which of the
following cellular processes or enzymes?

(B) DNA helicase
(C) Glucuronosyltransferase

(E) Ribosomal assembly

illness?
(A) Avoids the concern for reversion to virulence
(B) Develops more rapid protective immunity

her regimen, she also receives regular injections of a drug that induces reticulocyte release from the bone marrow

during a 15-minute session on a treadmill. The average pulse for the last 2 minutes of the session is 175/min. During

which of the following is most likely to be decreased?

owned swimming pool. He has no history of major medical illness and receives no medications. He appears tired.
His temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F); other vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows
conjunctival injection and discharge and oropharyngeal erythema. The public health department reports an outbreak

(A) Adenovirus
(B) Cytomegalovirus
(C) Epstein-Barr virus

and significant weight gain in her face and abdomen. Although her appetite has increased, she has noticed that her
arms and legs have become thinner. Which of the following additional findings are most likely in this patient?
(A) Hyperkalemia and numerous bruises
(B) Hypertension and muscle weakness
(C) Hypocalcemia and hyperglycemia
(D) Hypoglycemia and fat pads between the scapulae
(E) Jaundice and thinning of the skin

knee. His mother says, "He can usually walk around, but he hasn't been able to play in any of his soccer games since
this all began." Examination of the left knee shows warmth, swelling, and tenderness. An x-ray of the knee is shown.
Which of the following structures is attached to the abnormal anterior tibial area?

(A) Anterior cruciate ligament
(B) Gastrocnemius muscle
(C) Patellar ligament
(D) Popliteus muscle
(E) Posterior cruciate ligament

84/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no cyanosis. The
lungs are clear. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. Extremity examination shows no edema. The patient

epigastric tenderness. Genetic testing for the 36 most common mutations shows a detectable mutation (G551D) in

examination. Current medications include a short- acting β 2-adrenergic agonist by metered-dose inhaler as needed.

Physical examination shows no abnormalities. At the end of the examination, he tells the physician, "I enjoy coming
to see you because you remind me of my daughter. She died 35 years ago this month." He has been a patient of this
physician for 5 years. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?
(A) "I may have to refer you to another physician who doesn't remind you of your daughter so you can focus

(B) "I'd like to refer you to a grief counselor so that you can work out your unresolved feelings about your

(C) "I'm sorry you lost your daughter. Unfortunately, since we only have a limited amount of time, we must

ABSTRACT

The "Password Strength Checker" is a Java-based mini project designed
to evaluate the strength of a user’s password and provide suggestions
for improvement. In today’s digital world, creating secure passwords is
essential to protect personal and sensitive information from
unauthorized access. This project aims to help users understand how
strong their passwords are and how they can enhance security.
The application is developed using Java Swing to provide a simple and
user-friendly graphical interface. Users can enter a password, and the
system analyzes it based on various parameters such as length, use of
uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters. Based
on these factors, the password is categorized as Weak, Medium, or
Strong.

and color indicators, along with suggestions to improve the password

1. INTRODUCTION

In today’s digital era, the use of passwords has become an essential part of
securing personal and professional information. From social media accounts
to banking systems, passwords act as the first line of defense against
unauthorized access. However, many users tend to create weak passwords
that are easy to guess, making their data vulnerable to cyber threats.
The "Password Strength Checker" is a Java-based application developed to
address this issue by helping users evaluate the strength of their passwords.
This project aims to educate users about the importance of creating strong
and secure passwords by analyzing different aspects such as password
length, use of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special
characters.
The application is designed using Java Swing to provide a simple and
interactive graphical user interface. It allows users to input a password and
instantly receive feedback on its strength, categorized as Weak, Medium, or

This project not only enhances awareness about cybersecurity but also

serves as a useful tool for both learning and real-world application.

2. OBJECTIVE OF THE PROJECT
The main objectives of the "Password Strength Checker" project
are as follows:
• To design and develop a user-friendly application that
evaluates the strength of a password.
• To help users understand the importance of creating strong

• To analyze passwords based on different parameters such as
length, uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special

• To categorize passwords into different levels such as Weak,

3. METHODOLOGY / ALGORITHM

The "Password Strength Checker" project follows a simple and structured
methodology to evaluate the strength of a user’s password. The working
of the system is based on predefined rules and logical conditions.
Methodology:
The application is developed using Java Swing to create a graphical user
interface. The user enters a password in the input field, and upon clicking
the "Check" button, the system analyzes the password based on various
criteria such as length, characters used, and complexity. The result is then
displayed using labels and a progress bar along with color indicators.
Algorithm:
Step 1: Start the program.
Step 2: Create the GUI components such as window, labels, password
field, button, and progress bar.
Step 3: Accept the password input from the user.
Step 4: Initialize variables to check different conditions:
- Length of password
- Presence of uppercase letters
- Presence of lowercase letters
- Presence of digits
- Presence of special characters

Step 4: Initialize variables to check different conditions:
- Length of password
- Presence of uppercase letters
- Presence of lowercase letters
- Presence of digits
- Presence of special characters
Step 5: Check the length of the password:
- If length < 6 → Weak
- If length ≥ 6 → proceed to further checks
Step 6: Check character conditions:
- If only letters → Weak
- If letters + numbers → Medium
- If uppercase + lowercase + numbers + special characters and length ≥ 8
→ Strong
Step 7: Assign strength level (Weak, Medium, Strong).
Step 8: Update UI:
- Display strength text

- Change color (Red / Orange / Green)
- Update progress bar value
Step 9: Display suggestions:
- Add uppercase letters if missing
- Add numbers if missing
- Add special characters if missing
- Increase length if required
Step 10: End the program.
This methodology ensures that the password is evaluated efficiently and
provides instant feedback to the user for improving password security.

Executive summary
The Nineteenth Meeting of the WHO South -East Asia Regional Certification Commission for
Poliomyelitis Eradication (SEA-RCCPE) was held in Colombo, Sri Lanka, from 24 to 26 June 2026.
The Commission reviewed annual reports , for the year 2025, from National Certification
Committees for Poliomyelitis Eradication (NCCPEs), country presentations and regional programme
data to assess progress in sustaining the Region’s polio -free status and to review developments
related to population immunity, sur veillance, outbreak preparedness and response, poliovirus
containment, and polio transition.
The Commission concluded that the WHO South -East Asia Region continues to maintain its
wild poliovirus-free status. It acknowledged the sustained commitment of Member States, NCCPEs,
surveillance networks, laboratories and partners in protecting this achie vement and maintaining
strong programme performance across the Region.

metadata.title: SEA  HDC 5 eng
metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365
metadata.subject: SEA-RCCPE, polio eradication, 19th meeting, Colombo, Sri Lanka

page_content:
surveillance networks, laboratories and partners in protecting this achie vement and maintaining
strong programme performance across the Region.
The Commission noted that regional population immunity remains generally high and that
surveillance systems continue to provide a strong platform for the early detection of poliovirus
transmission. However, important immunity gaps persist among zero -dose and under-immunized
populations, hard-to-reach communities, migrant and displaced populations, and areas with long -
standing subnational disparities in vaccination coverage. The Commission further noted that three
countries in the Region have not yet introduced a second dose of inactivated poliovirus vaccine
(IPV2), which may lead to suboptimal population immunity against poliovirus type 2. The
Commission also noted continuing operational challenges in surveillance, including variations in
AFP detection, stool adequacy, timeliness of reporting and specimen transport in some countries.

metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365
metadata.subject: SEA-RCCPE, polio eradication, 19th meeting, Colombo, Sri Lanka

page_content:
Commission also noted continuing operational challenges in surveillance, including variations in
AFP detection, stool adequacy, timeliness of reporting and specimen transport in some countries.
The meeting reviewed recent variant poliovirus detections in the Region and noted that all
events were identified through sensitive surveillance systems and followed by timely investigations
and response measures. While these responses demonstrated the eff ectiveness of existing
surveillance and response mechanisms, they also highlighted the need for continued vigilance and
sustained programme performance.
The Commission further reviewed progress in poliovirus containment and polio transition.
While containment activities are generally progressing well across the Region, country-specific gaps
remain, including the need for updated facility inventories, stren gthened containment structures
and continued compliance with GAPIV requirements. Progress in transitioning essential polio

metadata.title: SEA  HDC 5 eng
metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365
metadata.subject: SEA-RCCPE, polio eradication, 19th meeting, Colombo, Sri Lanka

page_content:
remain, including the need for updated facility inventories, stren gthened containment structures
and continued compliance with GAPIV requirements. Progress in transitioning essential polio
functions into national health systems was also reviewed. Although some advances have been made,
transition milestones remain behind schedule in several priority countries, raising concerns about
the long -term sustainability of surveillance, laboratory and outbreak response capacities in the
context of declining external financing and the increasing risk of losing trained and experienced
human resources before their functions are fully institutionalized within national health systems.
The Commission recommended that Member States, with the continued support of partners
and other stakeholders, continue to strengthen routine immunization and surveillance, particularly
at subnational level; review and optimize polio vaccine schedules in line with WHO and SAGE

page_content:
1. Introduction
The WHO South -East Asia Region was certified polio -free by the South-East Asia Regional
Certification Commission for Poliomyelitis Eradication (SEA-RCCPE) in March 2014 and has since
maintained its status as free of indigenous wild poliovirus transmission. Sustaining this
achievement remains a major public health priority for Member States, particularly in the context
of continued wild poliovirus transmissi on in endemic countries, ongoing outbreaks of circulating
vaccine-derived polioviruses (cVDPVs ) in several regions, increasing population mobility,
humanitarian emergencies, and persistent immunity gaps among vulnerable populations. The
maintenance of polio-free status therefore requires sustained high population immunity, sensitive
surveillance systems, effective outbreak preparedness and response, and rigorous implementation
of poliovirus containment measures.
The global Polio Eradication Strategy (2022 –2029) continues to provide the overarching

metadata.title: SEA  HDC 5 eng
metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365
metadata.subject: SEA-RCCPE, polio eradication, 19th meeting, Colombo, Sri Lanka

page_content:
of poliovirus containment measures.
The global Polio Eradication Strategy (2022 –2029) continues to provide the overarching
framework for achieving and sustaining global polio eradication. As the global programme advances
towards eradication and eventual cessation of oral polio vaccines, countries are increasingly
required to strengthen preparedness for the post-eradication era. This includes maintaining highly
sensitive surveillance systems capable of rapidly detecting any poliovirus event, implementing
robust outbreak response mechanisms, and ensuring full compliance with the Global Action Plan for
Poliovirus Containment (GAPIV). Consequently, containment has become an essential component of
certification activities and a critical requirement for safeguarding the gains achieved through polio
eradication.
In parallel, countries in the Region are navigating the transition of polio assets and functions

metadata.title: SEA  HDC 5 eng
metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365
metadata.subject: SEA-RCCPE, polio eradication, 19th meeting, Colombo, Sri Lanka

page_content:
eradication.
In parallel, countries in the Region are navigating the transition of polio assets and functions
as external financing for polio eradication gradually declines. The polio transition agenda seeks to
ensure that critical capacities developed through the erad ication programme —particularly
surveillance, laboratory networks, outbreak preparedness and response, data systems, workforce
capacity and community engagement mechanisms—are sustainably integrated into national health
systems. Successful transition is ess ential not only for maintaining a polio -free Region but also for
protecting broader health security gains and supporting the delivery of other public health
priorities.
The Regional Vaccine Implementation Plan (RVIP), which serves as the regional framework
for implementing the goals of Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030), provides an important
framework for sustaining and maximizing the benefits of investments made through the polio

metadata.title: SEA  HDC 5 eng
metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365
metadata.subject: SEA-RCCPE, polio eradication, 19th meeting, Colombo, Sri Lanka

page_content:
for implementing the goals of Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030), provides an important
framework for sustaining and maximizing the benefits of investments made through the polio
programme. The essential capacities established through polio eradication contribute directly to
IA2030 and RVIP objectives by strengthening routine immunization systems and reaching
underserved populations to provide equitable access to immunization services (Strategic Priority
3: Coverage and Equity), vaccine-preventable disease surveillance, laboratory networks, outbreak
preparedness( Strategic Priority 6: Outbreaks and Emergencies) , risk assessment, and data use for
evidence based decision making , (Strategic Priority 7: Research, Innovation and Data) .. The
continuation and integration of these functions are therefore critical for achieving regional
immunization goals and advancing universal access to life-saving vaccines.

page_content:
The South-East Asia Region has consistently emphasized the importance of integrating polio
essential functions into broader immunization and health system agendas. Surveillance systems
originally established for polio are increasingly supporting integrated vaccine-preventable disease
surveillance, environmental surveillance platforms are contributing to broader public health
monitoring, and laboratory networks are strengthening capacity for detection of multiple
pathogens. Sustaining these assets through effective transition planning is therefore closely aligned
with both regional immunization priorities and wider health system strengthening efforts.
The SEA -RCCPE plays a critical role in supporting these objectives through independent
oversight of regional and national efforts to maintain polio -free status. The Commission reviews
annual reports submitted by National Certification Committees for Polio Eradication (NCCPEs),

page_content:
oversight of regional and national efforts to maintain polio -free status. The Commission reviews
annual reports submitted by National Certification Committees for Polio Eradication (NCCPEs),
assesses evidence related to population immunity, surveillance quality, outbreak preparedness,
containment and transition, and provides recommendations to Member States and WHO. Through
this process, the Commission contributes to the dual objectives of sustaining a polio-free Region and
ensuring that the investments and capacities developed through the Global Polio Eradication
Initiative continue to support regional immunization goals and public health priorities. The
Nineteenth Meeting of the SEA-RCCPE was convened in Colombo, Sri Lanka, from 24 to 26 June 2026.
2. Objectives of the meeting
The primary objective of the meeting was to assess progress in sustaining the wild
poliovirus-free status of the South -East Asia Region and to provide the Commission with a

▪ Outbreak preparedness and response
▪ Containment and post-certification strategy

• Accountability

3. Organization of the meeting
The meeting was inaugurated by the Deputy Minister of Health and Mass Media, Government
of Sri Lanka , along with the Acting WHO Representative to Sri Lanka and the Chair of the Global
Certification Commission for Poliomyelitis Eradication. The agenda included opening and closing
sessions, global and regional updates, country presentations by NCCPEs, containment updates, a
consultation on the polio transition, updates from the Eastern Mediterranean and Western Pacific
Regions, and closed-door deliberations by SEA-RCCPE members and the Secretariat.
The meeting brought together the SEA -RCCPE Chair and members, representatives of
NCCPEs, National Containment Task Forces and National Authorities for Containment, the polio
laboratory network, the Ministry of Public Health of Sri Lanka as host country, pa rtner agencies,

laboratory network, the Ministry of Public Health of Sri Lanka as host country, pa rtner agencies,

The meeting followed a three -day structure. Day 1 focused on global and regional updates
and initial country reviews. Day 2 continued NCCPE reviews and reviewed containment. Day 3
focused on the polio transition, inter -regional updates, closed -door deliberations, and the
presentation of conclusions and recommendations.
4. Methodology of the regional review
The regional review was based on annual progress reports for 2025 submitted by NCCPEs,
country presentations during the meeting, containment updates, regional and global surveillance
and programme data, and discussions among Commission members, NCCPE representatives and
the Secretariat.

5. Situation update and issues reviewed
5.1 Global and regional risk context
The global update highlighted that the international spread of poliovirus continues to
constitute a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, with ongoing WPV1 transmission in
Afghanistan and Pakistan, continued cVDPV outbreaks across multiple regions, and poliovirus
detections in countries using IPV -only schedules. Despite progress in reducing poliovirus

metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365

page_content:
Afghanistan and Pakistan, continued cVDPV outbreaks across multiple regions, and poliovirus
detections in countries using IPV -only schedules. Despite progress in reducing poliovirus
transmission, persistent immunity gaps, uneven surveillance performance and a challenging global
funding environment underscore the need to sustain eradication -level programme performance
until global eradication is achieved.
The regional update emphasized that the South -East Asia Region remains polio -free;
however, continued vigilance is required because of the ongoing risk of poliovirus importation,
recent variant poliovirus detections, subnational immunity gaps, uneven IPV c overage, delayed
introduction of a second IPV dose in three countries, and sustainability challenges associated with
transition and declining external financing.
5.2 Population immunity
The regional update reviewed polio vaccine schedules across countries. All countries except

transition and declining external financing.
5.2 Population immunity
The regional update reviewed polio vaccine schedules across countries. All countries except
Democratic People’s Republic of Korea are providing both bOPV and IPV. Four countries are
providing at least two doses of fractional IPV (fIPV): Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Sri Lanka. Three
countries are providing two full doses of IPV: Bhutan, Myanmar and Thailand. Democratic People’s
Republic of Korea, Maldives and Timor-Leste were noted as countries yet to introduce IPV2.

 The latest WHO and UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC)
showed the WHO South -East Asia Region as the highest performing among the six WHO regions,
sustaining high routine immunization coverage across key childhood vaccines. In 2025, DTP3 and
IPV1 coverages were 94% and IPV Complete Series (IPVC) coverage was 77%. While coverage data
indicated strong regional performance overall, important country and subnational variations
remain. An estimated 1.2 million children in the Region did not receive the DTP1 vaccine in 2025.
Myanmar and Timor-Leste continued to show lower coverage than most other countries.
5.3 Surveillance and laboratory performance
Regional surveillance sensitivity was maintained, although national and subnational
variations remained. Regional non -polio AFP rate was reported as 4.83 in 2025 and 2.88 in 2026,

variations remained. Regional non -polio AFP rate was reported as 4.83 in 2025 and 2.88 in 2026,
based on data available as of 22 June 2026. The percentage of adequate stool specimen collection
for the Region was 90% in both 2025 and 2026. Some AFP cases were noted as pending final
classification.
Environmental surveillance included 101 sites in five countries. The countries with
environmental surveillance included Bangladesh, India, Myanmar, Nepal and Thailand.
Environmental surveillance performance varied by country and year, and the Commission
emphasized the need for feasibility assessment and optimization based on epidemiological risk.
Laboratory indicators reviewed by the meeting showed approximately 52,000 AFP
specimens and approximately 2200 environmental surveillance samples tested in 2025. More than
97% of primary isolation results were available within 14 days, approximately 450 po liovirus

5.4 Poliovirus containment
The containment sessions reviewed global containment strategy, national inventories,
poliovirus-essential facilities, and regional containment progress. Containment implementation in
the Region was assessed as mostly on track, while country -specific issues remained. The
Commission emphasized that national facility inventories should be updated and that countries
should establish or strengthen NCTFs or NACs as appropriate.
• Countries were reminded of the need to maintain updated inventories of facilities retaining

5.5 Polio transition
The meeting reviewed the regional polio transition strategy and country progress. Four
countries in the Region are priority countries for polio transition: Bangladesh, India, Myanmar and
Nepal. Three countries have moved from the global transition priority list to the watch list, while
Myanmar remains on the priority list. The transition context is shaped by variable country
readiness, declining external funding and the need to sustain essential polio functions.
The regional transition strategy uses a three -pronged approach: human resource
mainstreaming, functional transition and financial sustainability. The strategy promotes phased,
risk-based and country-specific pathways, recognizing differences in epidemiological, political and
health system contexts across countries. The meeting emphasized that transition should not be seen
as an exit strategy but as a sustainability strategy to protect polio gains and integrate essential

health system contexts across countries. The meeting emphasized that transition should not be seen
as an exit strategy but as a sustainability strategy to protect polio gains and integrate essential
functions into broader health systems.
The draft regional transition strategy was shared with participants, who were organized into
country-specific groups and given a template to provide their inputs. All country groups submitted
completed templates to the Secretariat, and these inputs will inform finalization of the strategy.

6. Conclusions and recommendations
6.1 Overarching conclusions by SEA-RCCPE
The WHO South -East Asia Region continues to maintain its wild poliovirus -free status,
despite a challenging global epidemiological environment characterized by the continued
circulation of wild poliovirus type 1 in endemic countries and ongoing outbreaks o f circulating
vaccine-derived polioviruses in multiple regions of the world. The Commission noted that the
international spread of poliovirus remains a Public Health Emergency of International Concern and
emphasized that all countries in the Region must remain vigilant against the risk of importation and
subsequent transmission.

The Commission acknowledged the sustained commitment of Member States, National
Certification Committees for Polio Eradication (NCCPEs), national immunization programmes,
surveillance systems, laboratories and partners in maintaining the Region’s polio -free status. The
annual reports submitted by all Member States demonstrated continued efforts to sustain
population immunity, strengthen surveillance systems, improve outbreak preparedness and
response capacities, and implement poliovirus containment activities. The Commission appreciated
the progress made by countries in implementing recommendations from pre vious meetings and
endorsed the conclusions and recommendations of the respective NCCPEs.
The Commission noted that regional population immunity remains generally strong, with all
countries except Democratic People’s Republic of Korea implementing both bOPV and IPV
schedules, and all but three countries having introduced two-dose IPV schedules in line with SAGE

schedules, and all but three countries having introduced two-dose IPV schedules in line with SAGE
recommendations. Nevertheless, important immunity gaps continue to persist within and between
countries. Particular concern was expressed regardi ng sub optinsal coverage of IPV2 dose, zero-
dose and under -immunized populations, hard -to-reach communities, migrant and displaced
populations, and areas with longstanding subnational inequities in vaccination coverage. These
immunity gaps increase the risk of poliovirus emergence and transmission if virus importation were
to occur.
The Commission reviewed recent detections of variant polioviruses in the Region and noted
that all events were detected through sensitive surveillance systems and were followed by timely
public health investigations and response measures. The Commission appreciated the rapid actions

effectiveness of the Region’s surveillance and response capacities. However, the occurrence of these
detections also highlighted th e continued vulnerability of the Region and the need to sustain high
levels of surveillance and population immunity.
The Commission concluded that surveillance systems across the Region remain generally
sensitive and continue to perform well at national level. AFP surveillance, environmental
surveillance and laboratory networks collectively provide a strong platform for early detection of
poliovirus transmission. However, significant operational challenges remain. Subnational variability

persists in several countries, and gaps continue to be observed in AFP detection, stool adequacy,

The Commission recognized the important contribution of environmental surveillance and
laboratory networks in the Region. Environmental surveillance now operates in five countries with
more than one hundred surveillance sites, while regional laboratories c ontinue to meet high
performance standards and provide timely and reliable results. Nevertheless, further optimization
and expansion of environmental surveillance based on epidemiological risk will be important to

The Commission also reviewed progress in polio transition and noted that the four transition
priority countries in the Region —Bangladesh, India, Myanmar and Nepal —remain at different
stages of implementation. While progress has been observed in integrating selected polio functions
into broader health systems and government structures, transition milestones remain behind
schedule in several countries. The Commission expressed concern that declining external financing,
competing public health priorities and inadequate domestic resource mobilization could
compromise the sustainability of essential polio functions if transition is not adequately planned
and financed.
The Commission recognized that the Region is entering a particularly critical phase of the
eradication programme. In addition to risks associated with persistent WPV1 transmission globally

The Commission recognized that the Region is entering a particularly critical phase of the
eradication programme. In addition to risks associated with persistent WPV1 transmission globally
and continued cVDPV outbreaks, Member States face challenges related to containment compliance,
preparation for the post -eradication era, evolving immunization schedules, and sustainability of
polio-funded assets. The Commission emphasized that maintaining a polio-free Region will require
continued political commitment, sustained investment in immunization and surveillance systems,
effective outbreak preparedness and response mechanisms, and successful integration of essential
polio functions into resilient national health systems.

Nevertheless, the SEA-RCCPE expressed concern regarding low coverage of the third dose of
oral polio vaccine and the persistence of immunity gaps among certain population groups
The SEA-RCCPE recommended:
• timely follow-up on the implementation of the recommendations of the independent external
EPI and VPD surveillance review.
• strengthening routine immunization to address immunity gaps, especially among migrants
and low-coverage areas.
Timor-Leste
The SEA-RCCPE noted that a joint external EPI and VPD surveillance review was conducted
in 2024 and acknowledged the country's efforts to strengthen programme performance.
However, the Commission expressed concern that immunization coverage remains low. The
SEA-RCCPE further observed that surveillance performance remains suboptimal, as reflected by low
AFP detection rates and the absence of environmental surveillance.
The Commission also noted that containment structures remain inadequate and that there

The Commission also noted that containment structures remain inadequate and that there
is currently no National Containment Task Force in the country.
The SEA-RCCPE recommended:
• follow-up on the implementation of the joint external EPI -VPD Surveillance review with
prioritization on
o urgently strengthening immunization coverage and reaching zero-dose populations.
o strengthening surveillance systems and improving AFP detection rates.
• strengthening containment by establishing NCTF and conducting national facility survey.

Annex 2: Message from OIC
Nineteenth Meeting of the SEA Regional Certification Commission for Poliomyelitis Eradication
(SEA-RCCPE)
24 June 2026, Colombo, Sri Lanka
Honourable representatives of the Ministry of Health of Sri Lanka, Chair and Members of the South-
East Asia Regional Certification Commission for Poliomyelitis Eradication , Chairs and members of
National Certification Committees, Representatives of partner agencies, National Containment Focal
Points, Colleagues.
Good morning.
I am pleased to address this 19th meeting of the South-East Asia Regional Certification Commission
for Poliomyelitis Eradication.
To the newly appointed members of the Commission – welcome.
To the outgoing members – my thanks and appreciation for your dedication and service.
South-East Asia’s certification as polio -free in March 2014 was a landmark public health
achievement and a testament to what sustained commitment and collective action can accomplish.

metadata.title: SEA  HDC 5 eng
metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365
metadata.subject: SEA-RCCPE, polio eradication, 19th meeting, Colombo, Sri Lanka

page_content:
South-East Asia’s certification as polio -free in March 2014 was a landmark public health
achievement and a testament to what sustained commitment and collective action can accomplish.
Sustaining that achievement has depended on the diligence, technical judgement, and vigilance of
this Commission, whose work continues to protect one of the Region’s most valuable public health
gains.
But polio is not yet history.
Wild poliovirus type 1 continues to circulate in some countries.
Outbreaks of circulating vaccine -derived poliovirus, particularly type 2, have affected multiple
regions.
In an interconnected world, any outbreak anywhere can become a threat everywhere.
Immunity and surveillance gaps —particularly among mobile, marginalized and hard -to-reach
populations—remain the openings through which this disease moves.
During the course of this meeting, the Commission will review the annual reports and supporting
evidence from our Member States.

metadata.title: SEA  HDC 5 eng
metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365
metadata.subject: SEA-RCCPE, polio eradication, 19th meeting, Colombo, Sri Lanka

page_content:
populations—remain the openings through which this disease moves.
During the course of this meeting, the Commission will review the annual reports and supporting
evidence from our Member States.
The guidance you provide will address the key pillars that keep our region polio-free.
First: maintaining high population immunity through routine immunization and targeted strategies
for underserved communities.
Second: sustaining sensitive acute flaccid paralysis and environmental surveillance.
Third: strengthening risk assessment.
Fourth: outbreak preparedness—ensuring readiness to respond swiftly and effectively if poliovirus
is detected.
Fifth: advancing containment of polioviruses, in line with the Global Action Plan for Poliovirus
Containment, fourth edition (GAPIV).
As our Region advances in laboratory strengthening, vaccine production and biomedical research,
the number and complexity of facilities handling polioviruses will increase.

page_content:
The responsibility to prevent a containment breach grows with it.
Finally: Ensuring a smooth and responsible polio transition.
Transition is not an administrative exercise.
It is about protecting what works —core surveillance functions, rapid response capacities, and the
laboratory networks that countries have built.
It is about retaining the community engagement platforms, the data systems, and the trained
workforce that underpins immunization and outbreak preparedness.
None of this must be lost.
Bangladesh, India, Myanmar and Nepal are the priority countries we have identified where the scale
of polio-funded assets and functions is substantial.
Careful planning is essential to avoid any loss of critical capacity in these countries.
We look forward to the Commission’s clear conclusions on the Region’s certification status, to
guidance that is actionable, and recommendations that are prioritized.
These are invaluable for WHO and Member States alike and will ensure that our collective

metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365

page_content:
guidance that is actionable, and recommendations that are prioritized.
These are invaluable for WHO and Member States alike and will ensure that our collective
accountability remains strong.
My thanks to the Government and people of Sri Lanka, and the Ministry of Health, for graciously
hosting this meeting.
My thanks also to the Chair and members of the Commission for your continued independent
oversight; to the National Certification Committees, national containment authorities, and focal
points—for the rigour of your work throughout the year.
Together, let us continue to protect every child from poliomyelitis, and keep South-East Asia polio-
free.
Thank you.

The WHO South -East Asia Regional Certification Commission for Poliomyelitis Eradication (SEA -
RCCPE) provides independent oversight to the polio eradication programme in the South-East Asia Region.
The Commission meets annually to review reports submitted by the National Certification Committees
for Poliomyelitis Eradication (NCCPEs) of Member States, and to assess progress in maintaining wild
poliovirus-free status, monitoring vaccine-derived polioviruses, advancing poliovirus laboratory containment,
and implementing polio transition activities.
This report presents the conclusions and recommendations of the SEA-RCCPE from its nineteenth
meeting held in June 2026. The Commission concluded that the WHO South-East Asia Region maintains its
polio-free status and that there is no evidence of wild poliovirus (WPV) circulation in the Region.

Executive summary
The Nineteenth Meeting of the WHO South -East Asia Regional Certification Commission for
Poliomyelitis Eradication (SEA-RCCPE) was held in Colombo, Sri Lanka, from 24 to 26 June 2026.
The Commission reviewed annual reports , for the year 2025, from National Certification
Committees for Poliomyelitis Eradication (NCCPEs), country presentations and regional programme
data to assess progress in sustaining the Region’s polio -free status and to review developments
related to population immunity, sur veillance, outbreak preparedness and response, poliovirus
containment, and polio transition.
The Commission concluded that the WHO South -East Asia Region continues to maintain its
wild poliovirus-free status. It acknowledged the sustained commitment of Member States, NCCPEs,
surveillance networks, laboratories and partners in protecting this achie vement and maintaining
strong programme performance across the Region.

metadata.title: SEA  HDC 5 eng
metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365
metadata.subject: SEA-RCCPE, polio eradication, 19th meeting, Colombo, Sri Lanka

page_content:
surveillance networks, laboratories and partners in protecting this achie vement and maintaining
strong programme performance across the Region.
The Commission noted that regional population immunity remains generally high and that
surveillance systems continue to provide a strong platform for the early detection of poliovirus
transmission. However, important immunity gaps persist among zero -dose and under-immunized
populations, hard-to-reach communities, migrant and displaced populations, and areas with long -
standing subnational disparities in vaccination coverage. The Commission further noted that three
countries in the Region have not yet introduced a second dose of inactivated poliovirus vaccine
(IPV2), which may lead to suboptimal population immunity against poliovirus type 2. The
Commission also noted continuing operational challenges in surveillance, including variations in
AFP detection, stool adequacy, timeliness of reporting and specimen transport in some countries.

metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir

page_content:
Commission also noted continuing operational challenges in surveillance, including variations in
AFP detection, stool adequacy, timeliness of reporting and specimen transport in some countries.
The meeting reviewed recent variant poliovirus detections in the Region and noted that all
events were identified through sensitive surveillance systems and followed by timely investigations
and response measures. While these responses demonstrated the eff ectiveness of existing
surveillance and response mechanisms, they also highlighted the need for continued vigilance and
sustained programme performance.
The Commission further reviewed progress in poliovirus containment and polio transition.
While containment activities are generally progressing well across the Region, country-specific gaps
remain, including the need for updated facility inventories, stren gthened containment structures
and continued compliance with GAPIV requirements. Progress in transitioning essential polio

metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365

page_content:
remain, including the need for updated facility inventories, stren gthened containment structures
and continued compliance with GAPIV requirements. Progress in transitioning essential polio
functions into national health systems was also reviewed. Although some advances have been made,
transition milestones remain behind schedule in several priority countries, raising concerns about
the long -term sustainability of surveillance, laboratory and outbreak response capacities in the
context of declining external financing and the increasing risk of losing trained and experienced
human resources before their functions are fully institutionalized within national health systems.
The Commission recommended that Member States, with the continued support of partners
and other stakeholders, continue to strengthen routine immunization and surveillance, particularly
at subnational level; review and optimize polio vaccine schedules in line with WHO and SAGE

page_content:
1. Introduction
The WHO South -East Asia Region was certified polio -free by the South-East Asia Regional
Certification Commission for Poliomyelitis Eradication (SEA-RCCPE) in March 2014 and has since
maintained its status as free of indigenous wild poliovirus transmission. Sustaining this
achievement remains a major public health priority for Member States, particularly in the context
of continued wild poliovirus transmissi on in endemic countries, ongoing outbreaks of circulating
vaccine-derived polioviruses (cVDPVs ) in several regions, increasing population mobility,
humanitarian emergencies, and persistent immunity gaps among vulnerable populations. The
maintenance of polio-free status therefore requires sustained high population immunity, sensitive
surveillance systems, effective outbreak preparedness and response, and rigorous implementation
of poliovirus containment measures.
The global Polio Eradication Strategy (2022 –2029) continues to provide the overarching

metadata.title: SEA  HDC 5 eng
metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365
metadata.subject: SEA-RCCPE, polio eradication, 19th meeting, Colombo, Sri Lanka

page_content:
of poliovirus containment measures.
The global Polio Eradication Strategy (2022 –2029) continues to provide the overarching
framework for achieving and sustaining global polio eradication. As the global programme advances
towards eradication and eventual cessation of oral polio vaccines, countries are increasingly
required to strengthen preparedness for the post-eradication era. This includes maintaining highly
sensitive surveillance systems capable of rapidly detecting any poliovirus event, implementing
robust outbreak response mechanisms, and ensuring full compliance with the Global Action Plan for
Poliovirus Containment (GAPIV). Consequently, containment has become an essential component of
certification activities and a critical requirement for safeguarding the gains achieved through polio
eradication.
In parallel, countries in the Region are navigating the transition of polio assets and functions

metadata.title: SEA  HDC 5 eng
metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365
metadata.subject: SEA-RCCPE, polio eradication, 19th meeting, Colombo, Sri Lanka

page_content:
eradication.
In parallel, countries in the Region are navigating the transition of polio assets and functions
as external financing for polio eradication gradually declines. The polio transition agenda seeks to
ensure that critical capacities developed through the erad ication programme —particularly
surveillance, laboratory networks, outbreak preparedness and response, data systems, workforce
capacity and community engagement mechanisms—are sustainably integrated into national health
systems. Successful transition is ess ential not only for maintaining a polio -free Region but also for
protecting broader health security gains and supporting the delivery of other public health
priorities.
The Regional Vaccine Implementation Plan (RVIP), which serves as the regional framework
for implementing the goals of Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030), provides an important
framework for sustaining and maximizing the benefits of investments made through the polio

metadata.title: SEA  HDC 5 eng
metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365
metadata.subject: SEA-RCCPE, polio eradication, 19th meeting, Colombo, Sri Lanka

page_content:
for implementing the goals of Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030), provides an important
framework for sustaining and maximizing the benefits of investments made through the polio
programme. The essential capacities established through polio eradication contribute directly to
IA2030 and RVIP objectives by strengthening routine immunization systems and reaching
underserved populations to provide equitable access to immunization services (Strategic Priority
3: Coverage and Equity), vaccine-preventable disease surveillance, laboratory networks, outbreak
preparedness( Strategic Priority 6: Outbreaks and Emergencies) , risk assessment, and data use for
evidence based decision making , (Strategic Priority 7: Research, Innovation and Data) .. The
continuation and integration of these functions are therefore critical for achieving regional
immunization goals and advancing universal access to life-saving vaccines.

The South-East Asia Region has consistently emphasized the importance of integrating polio
essential functions into broader immunization and health system agendas. Surveillance systems
originally established for polio are increasingly supporting integrated vaccine-preventable disease
surveillance, environmental surveillance platforms are contributing to broader public health
monitoring, and laboratory networks are strengthening capacity for detection of multiple
pathogens. Sustaining these assets through effective transition planning is therefore closely aligned
with both regional immunization priorities and wider health system strengthening efforts.
The SEA -RCCPE plays a critical role in supporting these objectives through independent
oversight of regional and national efforts to maintain polio -free status. The Commission reviews
annual reports submitted by National Certification Committees for Polio Eradication (NCCPEs),

page_content:
oversight of regional and national efforts to maintain polio -free status. The Commission reviews
annual reports submitted by National Certification Committees for Polio Eradication (NCCPEs),
assesses evidence related to population immunity, surveillance quality, outbreak preparedness,
containment and transition, and provides recommendations to Member States and WHO. Through
this process, the Commission contributes to the dual objectives of sustaining a polio-free Region and
ensuring that the investments and capacities developed through the Global Polio Eradication
Initiative continue to support regional immunization goals and public health priorities. The
Nineteenth Meeting of the SEA-RCCPE was convened in Colombo, Sri Lanka, from 24 to 26 June 2026.
2. Objectives of the meeting
The primary objective of the meeting was to assess progress in sustaining the wild
poliovirus-free status of the South -East Asia Region and to provide the Commission with a

conclusion on the regional polio-free status.
The specific objectives of the meeting are enumerated below.

o To review country performances on maintaining polio -free status, based on reports
by National Certification Committees for Polio Eradication, with focus on :

▪ Polio surveillance;
▪ National risk assessments;
▪ Outbreak preparedness and response
▪ Containment and post-certification strategy
• Post-certification strategy:

of polioviruses
• Polio Transition

• Accountability

3. Organization of the meeting
The meeting was inaugurated by the Deputy Minister of Health and Mass Media, Government
of Sri Lanka , along with the Acting WHO Representative to Sri Lanka and the Chair of the Global
Certification Commission for Poliomyelitis Eradication. The agenda included opening and closing
sessions, global and regional updates, country presentations by NCCPEs, containment updates, a
consultation on the polio transition, updates from the Eastern Mediterranean and Western Pacific
Regions, and closed-door deliberations by SEA-RCCPE members and the Secretariat.
The meeting brought together the SEA -RCCPE Chair and members, representatives of
NCCPEs, National Containment Task Forces and National Authorities for Containment, the polio
laboratory network, the Ministry of Public Health of Sri Lanka as host country, pa rtner agencies,

NCCPEs, National Containment Task Forces and National Authorities for Containment, the polio
laboratory network, the Ministry of Public Health of Sri Lanka as host country, pa rtner agencies,
observers, WHO headquarters, WHO regional offices and WHO country offices.
The meeting followed a three -day structure. Day 1 focused on global and regional updates
and initial country reviews. Day 2 continued NCCPE reviews and reviewed containment. Day 3
focused on the polio transition, inter -regional updates, closed -door deliberations, and the
presentation of conclusions and recommendations.
4. Methodology of the regional review
The regional review was based on annual progress reports for 2025 submitted by NCCPEs,
country presentations during the meeting, containment updates, regional and global surveillance
and programme data, and discussions among Commission members, NCCPE representatives and
the Secretariat.

5. Situation update and issues reviewed
5.1 Global and regional risk context
The global update highlighted that the international spread of poliovirus continues to
constitute a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, with ongoing WPV1 transmission in
Afghanistan and Pakistan, continued cVDPV outbreaks across multiple regions, and poliovirus
detections in countries using IPV -only schedules. Despite progress in reducing poliovirus

metadata.title: SEA  HDC 5 eng
metadata.author: JOSHI, Sudhir
metadata.creator: Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365

page_content:
Afghanistan and Pakistan, continued cVDPV outbreaks across multiple regions, and poliovirus
detections in countries using IPV -only schedules. Despite progress in reducing poliovirus
transmission, persistent immunity gaps, uneven surveillance performance and a challenging global
funding environment underscore the need to sustain eradication -level programme performance
until global eradication is achieved.
The regional update emphasized that the South -East Asia Region remains polio -free;
however, continued vigilance is required because of the ongoing risk of poliovirus importation,
recent variant poliovirus detections, subnational immunity gaps, uneven IPV c overage, delayed
introduction of a second IPV dose in three countries, and sustainability challenges associated with
transition and declining external financing.
5.2 Population immunity
The regional update reviewed polio vaccine schedules across countries. All countries except

transition and declining external financing.
5.2 Population immunity
The regional update reviewed polio vaccine schedules across countries. All countries except
Democratic People’s Republic of Korea are providing both bOPV and IPV. Four countries are
providing at least two doses of fractional IPV (fIPV): Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Sri Lanka. Three
countries are providing two full doses of IPV: Bhutan, Myanmar and Thailand. Democratic People’s
Republic of Korea, Maldives and Timor-Leste were noted as countries yet to introduce IPV2.

 The latest WHO and UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC)
showed the WHO South -East Asia Region as the highest performing among the six WHO regions,
sustaining high routine immunization coverage across key childhood vaccines. In 2025, DTP3 and
IPV1 coverages were 94% and IPV Complete Series (IPVC) coverage was 77%. While coverage data
indicated strong regional performance overall, important country and subnational variations
remain. An estimated 1.2 million children in the Region did not receive the DTP1 vaccine in 2025.
Myanmar and Timor-Leste continued to show lower coverage than most other countries.

5.5 Polio transition
The meeting reviewed the regional polio transition strategy and country progress. Four
countries in the Region are priority countries for polio transition: Bangladesh, India, Myanmar and
Nepal. Three countries have moved from the global transition priority list to the watch list, while
Myanmar remains on the priority list. The transition context is shaped by variable country
readiness, declining external funding and the need to sustain essential polio functions.
The regional transition strategy uses a three -pronged approach: human resource
mainstreaming, functional transition and financial sustainability. The strategy promotes phased,
risk-based and country-specific pathways, recognizing differences in epidemiological, political and
health system contexts across countries. The meeting emphasized that transition should not be seen
as an exit strategy but as a sustainability strategy to protect polio gains and integrate essential

health system contexts across countries. The meeting emphasized that transition should not be seen
as an exit strategy but as a sustainability strategy to protect polio gains and integrate essential
functions into broader health systems.
The draft regional transition strategy was shared with participants, who were organized into
country-specific groups and given a template to provide their inputs. All country groups submitted
completed templates to the Secretariat, and these inputs will inform finalization of the strategy.

6. Conclusions and recommendations
6.1 Overarching conclusions by SEA-RCCPE
The WHO South -East Asia Region continues to maintain its wild poliovirus -free status,
despite a challenging global epidemiological environment characterized by the continued
circulation of wild poliovirus type 1 in endemic countries and ongoing outbreaks o f circulating
vaccine-derived polioviruses in multiple regions of the world. The Commission noted that the
international spread of poliovirus remains a Public Health Emergency of International Concern and
emphasized that all countries in the Region must remain vigilant against the risk of importation and
subsequent transmission.

The Commission acknowledged the sustained commitment of Member States, National
Certification Committees for Polio Eradication (NCCPEs), national immunization programmes,
surveillance systems, laboratories and partners in maintaining the Region’s polio -free status. The
annual reports submitted by all Member States demonstrated continued efforts to sustain
population immunity, strengthen surveillance systems, improve outbreak preparedness and
response capacities, and implement poliovirus containment activities. The Commission appreciated
the progress made by countries in implementing recommendations from pre vious meetings and
endorsed the conclusions and recommendations of the respective NCCPEs.
The Commission noted that regional population immunity remains generally strong, with all
countries except Democratic People’s Republic of Korea implementing both bOPV and IPV
schedules, and all but three countries having introduced two-dose IPV schedules in line with SAGE

countries. Particular concern was expressed regardi ng sub optinsal coverage of IPV2 dose, zero-
dose and under -immunized populations, hard -to-reach communities, migrant and displaced
populations, and areas with longstanding subnational inequities in vaccination coverage. These
immunity gaps increase the risk of poliovirus emergence and transmission if virus importation were
to occur.

The Commission also reviewed progress in polio transition and noted that the four transition

into broader health systems and government structures, transition milestones remain behind
